questions.stem: A 60-year-old patient with a history of smoking presents with progressive dyspnea and a chronic cough. Pulmonary function tests impaired expiratory flow. Chest imaging shows reveal hyperinflation. Which type of emphysema is most commonly associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
mum prevalence clinically.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Panacinar Emphysema: Panacinar emphysema involves the destruction of the entire respiratory acinus, including the respiratory bronchiole, alveolar ducts, and alveoli. It is often associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

 

Option C. Paraseptal Emphysema: Paraseptal emphysema, also known as distal acinar emphysema, involves the distal parts of the acinus, particularly the alveolar ducts and alveoli near the pleura. It often occurs adjacent to scars or fibrotic tissue, and it is associated with spontaneous pneumothorax.

 

Option D. Segmental Emphysema: Segmental emphysema refers to localized areas of emphysematous changes within a lung segment. It can occur in association with scarring or inflammation. While it is less common than other types of emphysema, it may contribute to localized airflow obstruction.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Centriacinar emphysema, is most commonly associated with cigarette smoking and predominantly affects the central parts of the acinus, leading to symptoms like progressive dyspnea and chronic cough in smokers.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 678)

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents with wheezing, shortness of breath, and cough. She has a history of asthma and is afebrile. On examination, her lungs show diffuse wheezing and decreased air entry. Which of the following chemical mediators is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of her inflammation?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Prostaglandins are eicosanoids derived from arachidonic acid that can cause vasodilation and increase the permeability of blood vessels. They can play a role in inflammation and are associated with pain and fever, but they are not the most significant mediators in bronchoconstriction associated with asthma.

 

Option C. Histamine is released by mast cells and plays a significant role in immediate hypersensitivity reactions. It can cause bronchoconstriction, increase vascular permeability, and cause smooth muscle contraction, but it is not the primary mediator in ongoing asthmatic responses.

 

Option D. IL-6 is a cytokine involved in the acute-phase reaction and plays a role in chronic inflammation and autoimmunity. While it is involved in systemic inflammation, it is not a major direct mediator of bronchoconstriction in asthma.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the context of asthma, leukotrienes are critical mediators that contribute to bronchial constriction, mucus secretion, and airway inflammation, leading to symptoms like wheezing and shortness of breath.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with a history of chronic cough and sputum production presents to the clinic. Pulmonary function tests reveal airway obstruction with a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. He reports a smoking history of 30 pack-years. Which of the following conditions is most likely contributing to an increased Reid's index in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
yle="font-size:12pt;">Explanation:

 

Option A: Bronchiectasis: In bronchiectasis, there is irreversible dilation of the bronchi. Reid's index is typically not a prominent feature in bronchiectasis.

 

Option B: Bronchial asthma: Asthma is characterized by reversible bronchoconstriction and inflammation. Reid's index is usually not significantly increased in bronchial asthma.

 

Option D: Emphysema: Emphysema is characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls, leading to airspace enlargement. Reid's index is not a characteristic feature of emphysema.

 

Educational objective:

 

Reid's index is a measure of the ratio of the thickness of the submucosal glands to the thickness of the bronchial wall that is a characteristic of chronic bronchitis.

 

Normal value: < 0.4

 

In chronic bronchitis: > 0.5 due to hypertrophy and hyperplasia of mucous glands

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 681)

Explanation:

Option C: Bronchiectasis: In bronchiectasis, there is irreversible dilation of the bronchi.

 

Option D: Emphysema is characterized by the destruction of alveolar walls and airspace enlargement.

The presence of Charcot-Leyden crystals and Curschmann's spirals in sputum is characteristic of bronchial asthma, reflecting eosinophilic inflammation and shedding of the bronchial mucosa, respectively, and are not typically found in chronic bronchitis, bronchiectasis, or emphysema.

questions.stem: A leading pharmacological company Cerebellum Pharma wants to manufacture drugs to treat bronchospasm seen in bronchial asthma. An antagonist of which of the mediators is likely to be effective in acute phase?
questions.solutionHtml:
physiology of acute asthma attacks.

Explanation:

Option A: Interleukin 5 (IL-5) is involved in the late phase reaction of asthma by promoting eosinophil activation and survival, but it is not a direct mediator of acute bronchospasm.

Option B: Platelet-activating factor (PAF) has a role in increasing vascular permeability and may contribute to inflammation associated with asthma, but it is not the primary mediator of acute bronchospasm.

Option D: Complement C3a is involved in the inflammatory response and can cause bronchospasm as part of an allergic reaction, but it is less specific to asthma than leukotrienes.

Educational Objective:

Leukotrienes C4, D4, and E4 are the key mediators of acute bronchospasm in bronchial asthma, which makes them a prime target for antagonism in the acute treatment of the disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following is TRUE regarding non- atopic asthma?
questions.solutionHtml:
allergic sensitization.

Explanation:

Option A: Allergen sensitization present – This typically pertains to atopic asthma, where there is a hypersensitivity reaction to environmental allergens, unlike non-atopic asthma.

Option B: Positive family history seen – While a positive family history can be a risk factor for asthma, it is more strongly associated with atopic rather than non-atopic asthma.

Option C: IgE levels raised – Elevated IgE levels are a hallmark of atopic asthma, which is associated with an allergic type of asthma and not commonly elevated in non-atopic asthma.

Educational Objective:

Non-atopic asthma is not primarily triggered by allergens and does not typically present with elevated IgE levels or allergen sensitization, but can be exacerbated by viral infections such as rhinovirus.

questions.stem: An elderly coal miner with a history of smoking and emphysema develops severe air-flow obstruction and expires. His autopsy reveals a “black lung,” with coal-dust nodules scattered throughout the parenchyma and a central area of dense fibrosis. The coal dust entrapped within this miner’s lung was sequestered primarily by which of the following cells?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option A. Endothelial cells line the blood vessels and are involved in the exchange of substances between the bloodstream and surrounding tissues.

 

Option B. Fibroblasts are the main cell type involved in tissue repair and fibrosis. In response to lung injury, they produce the extracellular matrix and collagen leading to fibrosis, but they do not phagocytose foreign materials such as coal dust.

 

Option C. Lymphocytes, including T and B cells, are primarily involved in the immune response against pathogens and are not known for phagocytosing materials like coal dust.

 

Educational Objective

 

In conditions such as coal workers' pneumoconiosis, also known as "black lung," macrophages are the primary cells responsible for sequestering coal dust. They phagocytose the dust particles and become the centre of coal-dust nodules, which may lead to lung fibrosis.



lects the inhalation of carbon particles. The characteristic pulmonary lesions of simple coal worker’s pneumoconiosis include non palpable coal-dust macules and palpable coal dust nodules, both of which are typically multiple and scattered throughout the lung as 1- to 4-mm black foci. These nodules have dust-laden macrophages associated with a fibrotic stroma. The other options are not phagocytic cells.

questions.stem: All of the following are seen in asbestosis except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

 

Option B: Calcified pleural plaques: This is a characteristic feature of asbestosis. Asbestos exposure can lead to the formation of pleural plaques, which are areas of fibrous thickening and calcification on the pleura. These plaques are a hallmark of asbestos-related lung disease.

 

Option C: Diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis: This is a correct option. Asbestosis is primarily characterized by the deposition of asbestos fibers in the lungs, leading to pulmonary fibrosis. It involves the interstitium of the lungs, causing scarring and impairment of lung function.

 

Option D: Mesothelioma: This is a correct option. Asbestos exposure is a well-established risk factor for the development of mesothelioma, a malignant tumor of the mesothelial cells lining the pleura, peritoneum, and other serosal surfaces.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Diffuse alveolar damage is not typically associated with asbestosis but is more indicative of acute conditions such as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), distinguishing it from the chronic fibrotic changes seen in asbestosis.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 672)



Robbins 10th/ 672)

Option A: Diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis: This is a characteristic feature of asbestosis. Prolonged exposure to asbestos fibers can lead to the development of diffuse interstitial fibrosis in the lungs.

Option B: Fibrous pleural thickening: Asbestos exposure can cause fibrous thickening of the pleura, the thin membrane covering the lungs and lining the chest cavity. This is a common finding in asbestosis.

Option D: Calcific pleural plaques: Calcific pleural plaques are a characteristic finding in asbestosis. These plaques are areas of calcification on the pleura and are often considered a hallmark of asbestos exposure.

Educational Objective:

Emphysema is not a feature typically associated with asbestosis but is instead related to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and smoking, due to the destruction of air sacs and decreased lung elasticity.

questions.stem: Gray hepatization of lungs is seen on which days:
questions.solutionHtml:
Ans. D. 5-7

 

Option D:

 

In the stages of bacterial pneumonia:

 

  1. Congestion (Day 1-2): The affected lobe becomes heavy and hyperemic due to increased blood flow. The alveoli are filled with organisms, fibrin, and bacteria.
  2. Red Hepatization (Day 2-4): The lung appears red and firm due to continued congestion. There is an influx of red blood cells (RBCs) and fibrin into the alveoli, leading to a solid, liver-like consistency.
  3. Gray Hepatization (Day 4-7): The red color fades, and the lung becomes gray-brown. This stage is characterized by ongoing inflammation, presence of fibrinopurulent exudate, and persistence of inflammatory cells.
  4. Resolution (beyond day 7): The inflammation gradually subsides, and macrophages clear the debris from the alveoli. The lung returns to normal architecture.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Gray hepatization of lungs is seen on day 5-7 of bacterial pneumonia.

 

(Ref: Harsh Mohan 6/e p469)



Harsh Mohan 6/e p469)

These symptoms were associated with a sharp, stabbing pain over her left lower chest that was worse when he took a deep breath. He was admitted to hospital with signs of septicaemia - high fever, increased heart rate (130/min) and decreased blood pressure (80/50). There was decreased air entry and a pleural rub over her left lower chest. She died on the same day. The presence of alveoli filled with exudates with the air being displaced converting the lung into a solid organ suggests which of the following diseases?
questions.solutionHtml:
trong>

 

Option D:

 

Explanation:

Option A: Chronic bronchitis: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by inflammation of the bronchi, leading to chronic cough and excessive mucus production. It does not typically result in the solidification of lung tissue.

Option B: Bronchial asthma: Asthma is characterized by reversible airway obstruction due to bronchospasm and inflammation. It does not cause the solidification of lung tissue seen in lobar pneumonia.

Option C: Bronchiectasis: Bronchiectasis involves the dilation and destruction of bronchi, leading to chronic cough and recurrent infections. While it can cause lung damage, it doesn't result in the same pattern of solidification as seen in lobar pneumonia

Educational Objective:

The presence of alveoli filled with exudates with the air being displaced converting the lung into a solid organ suggests lobar pneumonia.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th 708)




Robbins 10th 708)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old male with a history of smoking presents with a sudden onset of fever, productive cough, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest imaging reveals patchy infiltrates consistent with acute bronchopneumonia. On further evaluation, the patient develops worsening respiratory distress and signs of pleuritis. Which of the following complications is most likely to occur in this patient?

options.label: A
options.text: Cerebral infarction due to septic emboli

questions.solutionHtml:
g="EN-US" style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Septic emboli are not usually associated with bronchopneumonia, although sepsis can definitely occur in some patients.

Option B: Myocardial rupture is not a complication of acute bronchopneumonia.

Option C: Pulmonary emphysema is not a complication of bronchopneumonia.

Educational Objective:

Empyema is a potential complication of acute bronchopneumonia, which can occur when inflammation spreads to the pleural cavity, leading to the accumulation of pus in the pleural space.

 

Robbins 10th/ 708

questions.stem: A 56-year-old male patient with a history of alcoholism presents with a severe cough and production of copious amounts of mucoid sputum. A chest X-ray shows lobar consolidation. Which of the following pathogens is most likely to be responsible for this presentation?
questions.solutionHtml:
lidation on imaging.

Explanation:

Option A: Mycoplasma pneumoniae: This is a common cause of atypical pneumonia, particularly in younger populations. It often presents with a more insidious onset and is not typically seen on Gram stain. It does not respond well to beta-lactam antibiotics.

Option B: Legionella pneumophila: Legionella is another agent causing atypical pneumonia, often associated with contaminated water sources. It requires specialized culture conditions and is not seen on standard Gram stain, requiring silver staining for visualization.

Option C: Human coronavirus: Certain strains of coronavirus are known to cause respiratory illnesses ranging from the common cold to more severe diseases. These can result in atypical pneumonia, particularly in the setting of epidemics or pandemics.

Educational Objective:

Klebsiella pneumoniae is not a common cause of atypical pneumonia but rather causes classical lobar pneumonia, often associated with a severe course and production of thick mucoid sputum, particularly in patients with alcoholism or diabetes.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 708)



Robbins 10th/ 708)

questions.stem: A 35-year-old female presents with fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Which of the following chemical mediators is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of her acute inflammation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Leukotriene B4 (LTB4) is involved in the inflammatory process, mainly by attracting neutrophils to sites of inflammation. While it is a potent chemoattractant and can contribute to inflammation in the lungs, it is not the primary mediator in ARDS.

 

Option C. IL-1 is another important pro-inflammatory cytokine and plays a role similar to TNF-α in promoting inflammation. However, it is not as specifically implicated in ARDS as TNF-α.

 

Option D. Histamine is a mediator of allergic reactions and contributes to bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability. While histamine may be involved in the early stages of some types of lung injury, particularly those with an allergic or anaphylactic component, it is not the primary mediator in ARDS.

 

Educational Objective:

 

TNF-α is a critical mediator in the pathogenesis of acute lung injury and ARDS, promoting the recruitment of inflammatory cells to the lungs and contributing to the tissue damage and impaired gas exchange characteristic of these conditions.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old female presents with fever, cough, and shortness of breath. Her chest X-ray shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Which of the following factors in the coagulation cascade is most likely involved in the pathogenesis of her acute inflammation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Option A. Factor II, or prothrombin, is a plasma protein that is converted into thrombin in the coagulation cascade. Thrombin is a key enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, leading to clot formation. While it is central to the coagulation process, it is not known for initiating the inflammatory response in acute lung injury.

 

Option B. Factor V is a coagulation factor that works with factor X to convert prothrombin to thrombin. It is important in the progression of the coagulation cascade, but again, it is not specifically involved in the initiation of the inflammatory process in lung injury.

 

Option C. Factor VII is involved in initiating the extrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade upon tissue injury. While it is crucial for the body's response to vascular injury, it is not directly involved in the inflammation associated with acute lung injury.

 

Educational Objective:

 

In the context of acute lung injury, the activation of Factor XII can lead to the formation of fibrin clots in the pulmonary vasculature and contribute to the inflammatory response through the production of bradykinin.

questions.stem: Hyaline membrane disease is associated with:
questions.solutionHtml:
g normal gas exchange.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: Bronchopulmonary Dysplasia (BPD): Bronchopulmonary dysplasia is a chronic lung disease that can affect premature infants who have received mechanical ventilation and oxygen therapy for respiratory distress. It is characterized by inflammation and scarring in the lungs, leading to long-term respiratory problems.

 

Option C: Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS): Sudden Infant Death Syndrome is the sudden, unexplained death of an otherwise healthy infant, usually during sleep. It is not directly associated with hyaline membrane disease or the other respiratory conditions mentioned.

 

Option D: Bronchiolitis Obliterans: Bronchiolitis obliterans is a condition involving inflammation and scarring of the small airways (bronchioles) in the lungs. It can be associated with various causes, including infections and exposures to certain substances, but it is not specifically associated with hyaline membrane disease.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Respiratory Distress Syndrome, also termed hyaline membrane disease, is primarily caused by surfactant deficiency in premature infants, leading to the formation of hyaline membranes in the alveoli and subsequent respiratory distress.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 460)



Robbins 10th/ 460)

questions.stem: The percentage of pulmonary emboli, which proceed to infarction, is approximately:
questions.solutionHtml:
amily:"Calibri",sans-serif">Ans. B. 5-15%

Option B:

Explanation:

Pulmonary embolism (PE) occurs when a blood clot or other material lodges in the pulmonary arteries, blocking blood flow to a portion of the lung. Not all pulmonary emboli lead to infarction, which is the death of tissue due to a lack of blood supply. The likelihood of infarction depends on various factors, including the size and location of the embolus, the presence of collateral blood supply, and the overall health of the individual.

The majority of pulmonary emboli do not result in infarction, and the lung tissue supplied by the blocked artery may still receive enough blood from other vessels (collateral circulation) to prevent infarction.

Robbins direct quote.. ‘Only about 10% of pulmonary artery emboli actually cause infarction’.

Educational objective:

The percentage of pulmonary emboli that proceed to infarction is approximately 5-15%, taking into account the fact that the lung has a dual blood supply, from both the bronchial and pulmonary arteries. This collateral circulation often prevents infarction by continuing to supply the lung tissue with blood even when the pulmonary artery is obstructed.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 701)



Robbins 10th/ 701)

questions.stem: On sectioning of an organ at the time of autopsy, a focal, wedge-shaped firm area is seen accompanied by extensive hemorrhage, with a red appearance. The lesion has a base on the surface of the organ. This finding is typically of:
questions.solutionHtml:
l blood supply from the bronchial and pulmonary arteries, these infarcts are typically red (hemorrhagic).

Explanation:

Option B: Heart with coronary thrombosis typically results in pale (white) infarcts due to the loss of blood supply to the myocardium, unless reperfusion occurs, which can lead to a hemorrhagic appearance.

Option C: Liver with hypovolemic shock may not typically present with a wedge-shaped lesion but can show patchy necrosis due to global hypoperfusion.

Option D: Kidney with septic embolus can lead to infarcts that are generally pale (white) due to the organ's end-arterial blood supply, except in the case of a dual blood supply or reperfusion, which can lead to a hemorrhagic appearance.

Educational Objective:

Pulmonary thromboembolism is a condition that can present with a wedge-shaped, hemorrhagic (red) infarct on organ sectioning during autopsy, with the lesion's base on the organ surface.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 135)




Robbins 10th/ 135)

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year male was operated by hemicolectomy for adenocarcinoma colon. Post surgery he developed respiratory distress and a fall in p02 levels. He was intubated receiving mechanical ventilation with 100% oxygen. X ray chest shows opacity in all lung fields. A transbronchial lung biopsy has the following finding (image as shown). What is the likely mechanism underlying the above-described condition?

options.label: D
options.text: Release of fibrogenic cytokines by macrophages

questions.solutionHtml:
ltr" lang="EN-US" style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option B: Aspiration due to depressed cough reflex will lead to aspiration pneumonia.

Option A: DIC can complicate septic shock but not a primary cause of ARDS.

Option D: Release of fibrogenic cytokines causes diffuse fibrosis and not membrane deposition.

Educational Objective:

The injury to the alveolar-capillary endothelium is the hallmark of ARDS, which is characterized by an acute onset of diffuse pulmonary infiltrates and hypoxemia following a precipitating event such as surgery, trauma, or infection.

questions.stem: An infant born to a diabetic mother develops difficulty in breathing within 30 minutes of birth. Within a few hours, cyanosis becomes evident. Fine rales are heard over both lung fields. A chest x-ray film shows ground-glass picture. Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?

options.label: A
options.text: There is deficiency of surfactant produced by type Il alveolar cells

options.label: B
options.text: Increased corticosteroid release lower the risk of developing RDS

options.label: C
options.text: It is associated with respiratory failure and poor prognosis despite treatment

options.label: D
options.text: On microscopy, hyaline membranes with fibrin and necrotic cell debris are seen

questions.answerText: It is associated with respiratory failure and poor prognosis despite treatment
questions.solutionHtml:
span style="font-size:12pt">Explanation:

Option A: There is a deficiency of surfactant produced by type II alveolar cells – Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), also known as hyaline membrane disease, is indeed caused by a lack of surfactant, which is essential for decreasing surface tension in the alveoli.

Option B: Increased corticosteroid release lowers the risk of developing RDS – Corticosteroids stimulate the production of surfactant and are given to at-risk pregnant women to reduce the risk of RDS in premature infants.

Option D: On microscopy, hyaline membranes with fibrin and necrotic cell debris are seen – Microscopic examination of RDS typically shows hyaline membranes composed of fibrin and cellular debris lining the alveoli.

Educational Objective:

Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) is usually treatable with current medical interventions, and with prompt and appropriate management, it does not have to be associated with respiratory failure and poor prognosis.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 457



Robbins 10th/ 457

questions.stem: Which of the following is the characteristic feature of adult respiratory distress syndrome?
questions.solutionHtml:
and impaired gas exchange.

Explanation:

Option B: Interstitial tissue inflammation is a characteristic feature of viral pneumonia.

Option C: Alveolar exudates, such as protein-rich fluid, inflammatory cells, and debris, are indeed part of the pathology in ARDS. The alveoli become filled with these exudates, contributing to impaired gas exchange.

Option D: Interstitial fibrosis is a chronic, scarring process.

Educational Objective:

Diffuse alveolar damage is the hallmark histopathological finding in adult respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), characterized by damage to the alveolar walls, leading to increased permeability, pulmonary edema, and consequent impaired gas exchange.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient, previously treated for pulmonary tuberculosis, presents with cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. He has been diagnosed with reactivation of tuberculosis. This lesion is most likely to be located near:
questions.solutionHtml:
Option B. Near bronchus: TB can occur near bronchi, but reactivation often happens in areas with higher oxygen tension.

 

Option C. Subpleurally: TB can occur subpleurally, but reactivation is more common in areas with higher oxygen tension.

 

Option D. Base: The base of the lung has lower oxygen perfusion ratio, making it less favorable for reactivated TB.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Reactivated tuberculosis (TB) typically occurs in apex of lung.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th 370) 



Robbins 10th 370)

questions.stem: A healthcare worker with no known risk factors for tuberculosis (TB) receives a Mantoux test as part of a routine screening and returns to have the test read. The induration is noted to be less than 5 mm. What does this Mantoux test reading likely indicate?
questions.solutionHtml:
esponse in a patient with profound immunosuppression as seen in the patient of disseminated tuberculosis.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A. Tuberculous Infections: The Mantoux test measures cell-mediated immunity to tubercular antigens, and an induration of less than 5 mm typically does not suggest active tuberculosis infection in individuals without risk factors.

 

Option C. Decreased Susceptibility to Tuberculosis: A negative Mantoux test, defined as an induration of less than 5 mm in low-risk individuals, suggests that the person has not been sensitized to TB antigens and has not developed a measurable cell-mediated immune response. If it is due to immunosuppression, it is associated with increased (not decreased) susceptibity to tuberculosis.

 

Option D. Immunity to TB: The Mantoux test does not measure immunity to TB. A negative test does not imply immunity but rather that the individual has not had a prior infection that elicited a cellular immune response.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mantoux test Interpretation (for healthcare worker with no risk factors):

 

  • ≥15 mm → considered positive in low-risk individuals
  • ≥10 mm → considered positive in higher-risk groups (e.g., healthcare workers, recent immigrants, IV drug users)
  • ≥5 mm → positive in highest-risk groups (HIV-positive, close contacts of active TB, immunosuppressed)

 

A Mantoux test induration of less than 5 mm in an individual without risk factors is considered negative and suggests that the person has not been sensitized to TB antigens. It does not confirm active tuberculosis or immunity to TB.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presented with weight loss, low grade fever and cough with expectoration. Sputum testing for acid fast bacilli was positive, which of the following cytokines are involved in the pathogenesis of this disease:
questions.solutionHtml:
tyle="font-size:12pt">Option D. IL4 & IL 13 activated macrophages are alternatively activated macrophages and they are involved in tissue repair and termination of inflammation.

 

Option A. and B. They are anti-inflammatory cytokines

 

Educational Objective:

 

In tuberculosis, IFN-γ plays a crucial role in the activation of macrophages and the formation of granulomas, which are central to the body's defense against the bacilli.

 

Ref: Robbins 10th/ 98



Robbins 10th/ 98

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with a persistent cough, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss. Chest X-ray reveals an infiltrate in the upper lobe of the right lung. Which of the following is the earliest feature of tuberculosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
anuloma formation.

 

Explanation:

 

Option A: Caseation: Caseation, a form of necrosis typical of tuberculosis, is a later feature that occurs after the immune system has attempted to contain the infection.

 

Option C: Formation of giant cells (Langhans): Giant cell formation is part of the granuloma response and occurs after lymphocyte recruitment, as part of the body's attempt to wall off and contain the infection.

 

Option D: Granuloma formation: Granuloma formation is a hallmark of the body's defense against tuberculosis but is not the earliest event. It occurs after lymphocytes and macrophages have been recruited to the site of infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Recruitment of lymphocytes is the earliest feature in the immune response to M. tuberculosis infection. Following infection, lymphocytes are recruited, leading to the activation of macrophages and subsequent granuloma formation.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 378)



Robbins 10th/ 378)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient with suspected tuberculosis undergoes laboratory investigations. Which of the following statements regarding Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) in tuberculosis is accurate?

options.label: C
options.text: ESR is raised because of increased RBC aggregate

options.label: D
options.text: ESR is raised due to decreased RBC size

questions.answerText: ESR is raised because of increased RBC aggregate
questions.solutionHtml:
e="font-family:Aptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

Option A: This option suggests that tuberculosis does not affect the erythrocyte sedimentation rate. However, this is not accurate because ESR is known to be a non-specific marker of inflammation and can be elevated in various infectious diseases, including tuberculosis. ESR can rise due to the increase in plasma proteins, like fibrinogen and immunoglobulins, which promote erythrocyte aggregation.

Option B: This statement is not accurate as ESR is a non-specific test and cannot be used to confirm recovery from tuberculosis. While a decreasing ESR might be seen with clinical improvement, it is not definitive because many factors can influence ESR levels. Other diagnostic methods and clinical assessments are necessary to confirm recovery from TB.

Option D: This option is  ESR is not typically affected by the size of red blood cells directly; it is more influenced by the rate at which red blood cells aggregate and settle in a period. A decrease in RBC size (microcytosis) is more commonly associated with conditions such as iron-deficiency anemia rather than with changes in ESR.

Educational Objective:

An increased ESR in a patient with tuberculosis is due to the aggregation of red blood cells, known as rouleaux formation, facilitated by increased levels of fibrinogen and other acute-phase reactants. This is indicative of an active disease state but is not specific to tuberculosis, nor can it confirm recovery from the disease.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 378)



lection of the presence of an inflammatory process but is not specific to tuberculosis alone.

questions.stem: Which of the following occupational disease patients have an increased susceptibility to develop tuberculosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
ptos,sans-serif">Explanation:

Option A: Coal Workers Pneumoconiosis (CWP) is a lung disease caused by the inhalation of coal dust. While it primarily leads to respiratory symptoms and lung function impairment, it is not typically associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis.

Option B: Asbestosis is caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers, leading to interstitial fibrosis in the lungs. While asbestos exposure can increase the risk of developing certain respiratory conditions, it is not specifically associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis.

Option D: Bagassosis is a form of pneumoconiosis caused by the inhalation of moldy sugarcane dust. It is not typically associated with an increased susceptibility to tuberculosis.

Educational Objective:

Silicosis, a lung disease caused by inhaling crystalline silica dust, is associated with an increased risk of tuberculosis because silica particles can impair the lung's immune response, specifically the function of macrophages, making it a risk factor for the reactivation of latent tuberculosis infections.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 695)



Robbins 10th/ 695)

questions.stem: A medical resident is reviewing the pathology of tuberculosis (TB) with their attending. They are trying to differentiate the features of primary TB from secondary (reactivation) TB. Which of the following is least likely to be found in primary tuberculosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
the lungs.

 

Explanation:

 

Option B: Caseation: Caseation, which is a form of necrosis associated with TB, can occur in both primary and secondary tuberculosis as part of the granuloma formation process.

 

Option C: Calcification: Calcification in primary TB is part of the Ghon complex, representing healing and containment of the infection, often seen in primary TB lesions.

 

Option D: Langhans giant cell: Langhans giant cells are a type of multinucleated giant cell seen in granulomas and can be found in both primary and secondary TB as part of the body's immune response to the infection.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Cavitation is more frequently associated with secondary tuberculosis, where a previously sensitized host's immune response leads to caseous necrosis and cavity formation. This feature is less commonly observed in primary tuberculosis.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 375)



Robbins 10th/ 375)

questions.stem: A child presents to the OPD with proptosis. The mass responsible for same was biopsied and found to be a desmin positive tumor. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?

A 55-year-old patient presents with generalized tiredness, malaise, muscle weakness, and bone pain. Laboratory investigations reveal serum calcium to be 13 mg/dL. Which of the following lung cancers is implicated in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-size:11pt">Explanation:

Option A. Small cell carcinoma of the lung: Small cell carcinoma of the lung is more commonly associated with paraneoplastic syndromes like SIADH or Cushing's syndrome due to ectopic ACTH production, rather than hypercalcemia.

Option B. Adenosquamous carcinoma of the lung: Adenosquamous carcinoma of the lung can produce paraneoplastic syndromes, but it is not the most common type associated with hypercalcemia.

Option D. Large cell carcinoma of the lung: Large cell carcinoma can present with several paraneoplastic syndromes, but it is not the most frequent cause of paraneoplastic hypercalcemia.

Educational Objective:

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is frequently associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia, often due to the secretion of PTHrP, leading to elevated calcium levels that manifest with symptoms such as fatigue, muscle weakness, and bone pain.

 

Ref: Robbins and Cotran pathologic basis of disease 10th edition page: 329



Robbins and Cotran pathologic basis of disease 10th edition page: 329

questions.stem: All are true regarding mesothelioma except:
questions.solutionHtml:
pan style="font-size:12pt">Option B: Associated with asbestos exposure is correct. Mesothelioma has a well-established association with asbestos exposure, often presenting decades after initial exposure.

 

Option C: Histology shows a biphasic pattern is true for mesothelioma. Microscopically, it can exhibit both epithelioid and sarcomatoid features, hence referred to as biphasic.

 

Option D: Occurs in late middle age is also true. Mesothelioma typically presents in the mean age group of 50 to 70 years.

 

Educational Objective:

 

Mesothelioma is typically unilateral at presentation, not bilaterally symmetrical, and is associated with asbestos exposure, often presenting in late middle age with a histological biphasic pattern.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 735)



erred to as biphasic.

questions.stem: A 67-year male with history of chronic smoking hemoptysis with cough. Bronchoscopic biopsy from centrally located mass shows undifferentiated tumor histopathologically. Most useful I.H.C. (immunohistochemical) marker to make a proper diagnosis would be:
questions.solutionHtml:
EN-US" style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Option D: Hep par1 is a marker of liver cancer

Option B: TTF 1 is a marker of adenocarcinoma of the lung

Educational Objective:

The appropriate immunohistochemical marker for diagnosis of a centrally located bronchogenic carcinoma in a patient with a history of chronic smoking, is cytokeratin.

 

(Robbins 10th/ 720)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic lung disease presents with progressive dyspnea. Imaging reveals the presence of scar tissue in the lung parenchyma, likely a consequence of chronic inflammation and injury. Which of the following types of lung cancer is most commonly associated with chronic lung scarring and inflammation?
questions.solutionHtml:
Explanation:

Option B: Oat cell carcinoma, also known as small cell lung cancer, is strongly associated with smoking and typically arises in the central regions of the lungs. It is less likely to be associated with lung scarring compared to adenocarcinoma.

Option C: Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung often arises in the central part of the lungs and is linked to smoking. It may be related to chronic inflammation but is not typically associated with lung scarring as adenocarcinoma is.

Option D: Large cell cancer of the lung can appear in any part of the lung and tends to grow rapidly. Like squamous cell carcinoma, it is not primarily associated with pre-existing lung scarring.

Educational Objective:

Adenocarcinoma is the type of lung cancer most commonly associated with chronic lung scarring and inflammation, presenting as peripheral lung tumors that may arise from areas of scar tissue.

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 716)



Robbins 10th/ 716)

questions.stemHtml: A 70-year male, chronic smoker develops a non productive chronic cough since past 6 months. He also has weight loss, anorexia and chest pain. CT scan shows a mass lesion from which biopsy is taken (image given along side). Which of the statements best describes the above pathology?

options.label: D
options.text: Cells are p63 and p40 positive

questions.answerText: Cells are p63 and p40 positive
questions.solutionHtml:
strong> diagnosis of squamous cell carcinoma.

Explanation:

Option A: Pathology is peripheral in location – This would typically describe adenocarcinoma of the lung, not squamous cell carcinoma which commonly presents as a central lesion, especially in smokers.

Option B: More common in females – Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung has been historically more common in males, particularly those with a history of smoking.

Option C: Azzopardi effect is seen – This is characteristic of small cell carcinoma of the lung, where necrotic cells impart a basophilic staining to blood vessel walls, not squamous cell carcinoma.

Educational Objective:

Squamous cell carcinoma of the lung is commonly central in location, more prevalent in male smokers, and is characterized by cells that are p63 and p40 positive on immunohistochemical staining.

questions.stemHtml: A 56 year male smoker complains of weight loss, anorexia, chest pain and listlessness since 8 months. The following findings are noted in bronchioalveolar lavage fluid. Which of the following is LEAST LIKELY to be present with this pathology?
questions.solutionHtml:
t typically with small cell lung cancer.

Explanation:

Option A: Hyponatremia may be seen due to inappropriate ADH secretion by small cell carcinoma of the lung, which is known for paraneoplastic syndromes, including SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone).

Option B: Gynecomastia can result from ectopic gonadotropin production, which can occur with certain lung carcinomas such as small cell lung cancer.

Option D: Cushing's syndrome can be a manifestation of ectopic ACTH production by small cell carcinoma of the lung.

Educational Objective:

Hypercalcemia is typically associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung and is the least likely paraneoplastic syndrome to be associated with small cell lung cancer, which is more commonly related to ectopic production of ADH, ACTH, or gonadotropins.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman had complaints of enophthalmos, meiosis, anhidrosis and ptosis. X ray chest shows right upper lobe opacification with destruction of rib. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
>due to invasion of the cervical sympathetic chain and may cause rib destruction due to local invasion.

Explanation:

Option A: Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease that primarily causes bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and lung involvement, but it typically does not present with Horner's syndrome or rib destruction.

Option B: Tuberculosis can cause upper lobe opacities and cavitation, especially reactivation tuberculosis, but it is less likely to cause Horner's syndrome and rib destruction unless there is direct extension of the infection, which is rare.

Option D: Lobar pneumonia is an acute infectious process that affects a large and continuous area of the lobe of a lung. It generally presents with consolidation on imaging but does not cause Horner's syndrome or rib destruction.

Educational Objective:

Pancoast tumor is when a patient presents with symptoms of Horner's syndrome and imaging shows a lung lesion at the apex with associated bone destruction, which is not characteristic features of sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, or lobar pneumonia.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common symptom seen in patients with lung cancer?
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Explanation:

Option B: Dyspnea or shortness of breath is a common symptom but typically occurs later as the tumor grows or if there is involvement of the lung parenchyma, pleura, or lymphatic spread causing obstruction.

Option C: Weight loss is often a sign of systemic illness and can be present in lung cancer patients, especially as the disease progresses, due to cancer cachexia or tumor metabolism effects.

Option D: Chest pain may occur, particularly if the tumor invades the pleura or chest wall, but it is less common as an initial symptom compared to cough.

Educational Objective:

Cough is the most common presenting symptom in patients with lung cancer, which can be due to airway irritation or obstruction by the tumor.

 

Robbins 10th/ 721

questions.stem: A 66-year-old male with a clinical history of systemic hypertension and emphysema is brought to the emergency. He is a smoker for past 20 years. The physician examining him notices marked congestion of his head, neck, and upper extremities. Of the following, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solutionHtml:
style="font-family:"Calibri",sans-serif">Explanation:

Option A: Horner's syndrome is characterized by ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis, and enophthalmos due to disruption of the sympathetic nervous pathway, often without vascular congestion as described.

Option B: Aortic dissection may present with severe chest pain and can be catastrophic, but it would not typically cause congestion of the head, neck, and upper extremities.

Option C: Spontaneous pneumothorax presents with sudden chest pain and dyspnea. It is related to the collapse of a lung but would not cause upper body congestion.

Educational Objective:

The clinical presentation of superior vena cava syndrome, includes congestion of the head, neck, and upper extremities due to obstruction of venous return by a tumor or other mass.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with chronic cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. Imaging reveals a centrally located lung mass with evidence of cavity formation. Biopsy of the lesion confirms the diagnosis of bronchogenic carcinoma. Which type of bronchogenic carcinoma is most commonly associated with the observed cavity formation?
questions.solutionHtml:
os,sans-serif">Explanation:

Option B: Oat cell carcinoma, or small cell lung cancer, is highly aggressive and associated with smoking. However, it typically does not lead to cavitary lesions; instead, it is known for rapid growth and early metastasis.

Option C: Adenocarcinoma of the lung generally presents as peripheral lesions and is less likely than squamous cell carcinoma to present with cavitation.

Option D: Bronchoalveolar carcinoma, a subtype of adenocarcinoma, typically presents with a pneumonia-like consolidation rather than cavitation and is less related to smoking compared to other types.

Educational Objective:

 

 

(Ref: Robbins 10th/ 716)




Robbins 10th/ 716)

questions.stemHtml: A 58 year male factory worker complains of dyspnea along with chest pain and tiredness since 2 years. He also had a right sided pleural effusion which was drained. Patient died after 6 months. The appearance of his lung at autopsy is given in the image. Which statement regarding the pathology is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: History of prior treatment of TB is a usual finding

options.label: B
options.text: Can show both epitheloid and sarcomatous elements on histology

questions.answerText: Can show both epitheloid and sarcomatous elements on histology
questions.solutionHtml:

Option B:

The pathology shown here is of a malignant mesothelioma arising from pleura wherein the entire lung is encased in a thick greyish- white pleural tumour. Other features include

 

  • 20% of tumours show both epithelioid and sarcomatoid elements on histology. 
  • Deletion of  chromosome 9p is common.
  • There is NO increased risk of developing mesothelioma in pts’ of TB. 
  • It occurs mainly due to prolonged exposure with asbestos (shipping industry).
  • Mesothelioma DOESNOT elaborate ectopic hormones.

Educational Objective:

Malignant mesothelioma can histologically exhibit both epithelioid and sarcomatoid elements, which is a notable feature in approximately 20% of tumors, emphasizing the disease's diverse histological presentation.
